title: Expression Trees
summary: Treat a lambda as data you can inspect, build and translate, the way LINQ providers do.

steps.title: Code as data
body: The compiler turns the lambda into runnable code. You can call it, and that is all you can do. You cannot ask it *what* it checks.
Change only the type of the variable and something very different happens:

Now the compiler does **not** produce runnable code. It builds a small tree of objects that *describes* the lambda: a parameter called `age`, a constant `18`, and a *greater than or equal* node joining them. This is an **expression tree**.
A tree can still become code when you want to run it. `Compile()` turns it into an ordinary delegate:

steps.explain: The body is a *less than* node, the lambda has one parameter named `price`, and once compiled it is a normal function: 25 is not less than 10.

steps.title: Walking the tree
body: Every node in a tree derives from `Expression`. The lambda `p => p.Price > 18` is made of five nodes:
| Part of the code | Node class | What you can read |
`Body`, `Left` and `Right` are typed as plain `Expression`, so you cast or pattern match to see what is really there:
`NodeType` is an enum that says which operation a node is: `GreaterThan`, `Equal`, `AndAlso` (for `&&`), `OrElse` (for `||`), `Add`, and many more.

steps.prompt: In the tree for `p => p.Price > 18`, match each piece of code to the node class that represents it.

steps.title: Read a rule
prompt: Write `static string Describe(Expression<Func<int, bool>> rule)` that reads a simple comparison and returns `"<parameter name> <NodeType> <constant>"`.
You may assume the body is always *parameter, operator, constant*, in that order.
starter: // TODO: cast rule.Body, then read its Left, NodeType and Right
hints: The body of a comparison is a `BinaryExpression`: `var body = (BinaryExpression)rule.Body;`
Its `Left` is a `ParameterExpression` (read `Name`) and its `Right` is a `ConstantExpression` (read `Value`).

steps.title: Building a tree by hand
body: The compiler builds trees from lambdas. You can build the same trees yourself with the factory methods on `Expression`. This is how you create a filter whose shape is only known at run time, such as one assembled from a search form.
You work from the leaves up: parameters and constants first, then the nodes that combine them, and finally the lambda that wraps the body.
Use the **same** `ParameterExpression` object in the body and in the `Lambda` call. Two parameters with the same name are still two different parameters.
Other factories follow the same pattern: `Expression.Add`, `Expression.Multiply`, `Expression.Equal`, `Expression.LessThanOrEqual`, `Expression.AndAlso`, `Expression.OrElse`, `Expression.Property`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines to build `price => price > 100` by hand, compile it and try it on 250.
steps.explain: Leaves first (the parameter and the constant, in either order), then the comparison that joins them, then the lambda, then `Compile`.

steps.prompt: Build `x => x * 2` by hand so that the last line prints 42.
steps.explain: A parameter, a constant, a `Multiply` node joining them, a lambda around it, and `Compile` to get something you can call.

steps.title: Build a range check
prompt: Write `static Expression<Func<int, bool>> Between(int min, int max)` that **builds by hand** the tree for
- put `min` and `max` into the tree with `Expression.Constant`
- the lower check comes first, joined to the upper check with `Expression.AndAlso`
Writing a C# lambda and returning it will not pass: a lambda would capture the variables `min` and `max` instead of storing their values as constants.
starter: static Expression<Func<int, bool>> Between(int min, int max)
// TODO: build x >= min, build x <= max, join them with AndAlso
solution: static Expression<Func<int, bool>> Between(int min, int max)
template: Dojo.Eq("The body is an AndAlso node", ExpressionType.AndAlso, __rule.Body.NodeType);

Dojo.Check("min and max are constants in the tree", __rule.Body is BinaryExpression { Left: BinaryExpression { Right: ConstantExpression }, Right: BinaryExpression { Right: ConstantExpression } }, "Use Expression.Constant(min) and Expression.Constant(max).");
hints: `Expression body = Expression.AndAlso(lower, upper);` and keep the `return` line as it is.

steps.title: Why this exists: translating code
body: Why would anyone want a description of a lambda instead of the lambda? Because a description can be **translated into another language**.
This is how Entity Framework and other LINQ providers work:

`db.Products` is an `IQueryable<Product>`, and its `Where` takes an `Expression<Func<Product, bool>>`. The provider never runs your lambda. It walks the tree, writes `WHERE Price < 10`, and sends that to the database. Only the matching rows travel back.
The `Where` you know from lists is different: `IEnumerable<T>.Where` takes a plain `Func`. It can only run the lambda in memory, one item at a time.
A translator is a recursive method with one case per kind of node:
return $"({Translate(b.Left)} + {Translate(b.Right)})";    // handle both sides, then join
The `default` case matters. A real provider throws for C# it has no translation for, which is the error you get when you call one of your own methods inside an EF query.

steps.prompt: Why does `IQueryable<T>.Where` take an `Expression<Func<T, bool>>` and not a `Func<T, bool>`?
options: So the provider can inspect the condition and translate it, for example into SQL
Because expression trees run faster than delegates
So the lambda can be compiled twice for safety
steps.explain: A delegate is a sealed box: it can only be called. A tree can be read, so the provider can turn the condition into a `WHERE` clause and let the database do the filtering.

steps.title: A tiny SQL translator
prompt: Finish `Translate` so that `ToSql` turns a predicate over `Product` into SQL-like text. The tests have:
class Product { public string Category { get; set; }  public int Price { get; set; }  public int Stock { get; set; } }
Rules, one per kind of node:
- **`BinaryExpression`** becomes `(left OP right)`, where both sides are translated recursively and `OP` comes from the node type:
- **`ConstantExpression`** becomes its value. Strings go in single quotes: `'tea'`
starter: static string ToSql(Expression<Func<Product, bool>> predicate) => Translate(predicate.Body);
// TODO: case MemberExpression   -> the member's name
// TODO: case ConstantExpression -> the value, strings in single quotes
solution: static string ToSql(Expression<Func<Product, bool>> predicate) => Translate(predicate.Body);
template: void __Case(string name, string expected, Expression<Func<Product, bool>> predicate) =>
__Case("p => p.Stock <= 5 && p.Price >= 20", "((Stock <= 5) AND (Price >= 20))", p => p.Stock <= 5 && p.Price >= 20);
__Case("p => p.Category != \"gift\" || p.Stock < 1", "((Category <> 'gift') OR (Stock < 1))", p => p.Category != "gift" || p.Stock < 1);
__Case("p => p.Category == \"tea\" && (p.Price < 10 || p.Stock == 0)", "((Category = 'tea') AND ((Price < 10) OR (Stock = 0)))", p => p.Category == "tea" && (p.Price < 10 || p.Stock == 0));
Dojo.Throws<NotSupportedException>("A method call such as p.Category.StartsWith(\"t\") throws NotSupportedException", () => ToSql(p => p.Category.StartsWith("t")));
hints: Start with the two leaves. `case MemberExpression member: return member.Member.Name;` and for a constant, check `constant.Value is string text` to decide on quotes.
The binary case calls `Translate` on both sides: `$"({Translate(binary.Left)} {Operator(binary.NodeType)} {Translate(binary.Right)})"`.
Fill in `Operator` with one `case ExpressionType.X: return "...";` line per row of the table. `&&` is `AndAlso`, `||` is `OrElse`.
